discovery: Invention and realization of the optical lattice clock

nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics; precision measurement
motivation: Katori conceived the optical lattice clock (2001-2005): neutral atoms trapped in an optical lattice at a 'magic wavelength', where the light shifts of both clock states cancel, so that many atoms can be interrogated without motional or trap perturbations. Ye pushed the concept to its limits, using spin-polarized fermionic strontium, ultrastable lasers and control of atomic interactions to reach accuracy and stability at the 10^-18 level and beyond. Together they made optical clocks about a hundredfold better than caesium standards, prompting the planned redefinition of the SI second. These clocks now resolve gravitational redshift over millimetre height differences, enable relativistic geodesy, and provide tabletop tests of fundamental physics, including searches for dark matter, variations of constants and new forces. The magic-wavelength lattice has also become a basic tool across quantum simulation and neutral-atom quantum computing, opening a platform used by the whole community.
